title: Business as Usual / A Trannying Day Special
summary: Chapter 19 stages a cast-wide cross-dressing episode under a historical title containing a slur. The title and every spoken idea remain literal in the source layer; the editorial layer distinguishes gender expression from gender identity and does not infer that any participant is transgender. The comedy premise repeatedly collides with direct boundaries: one participant says he feels threatened, wants the clothes off, dislikes all of it, feels isolated, refuses Tinder and pleads not to wrestle. A photo-sharing request receives two no's. Later, sexualized attention continues after requests to stop, a shirt-removal prompt receives no, anal contact from an earlier encounter is recalled with surprise and protest, butt-contact games generate pain, and the person who caused pain apologizes. The archive keeps refusal, pressure, participation and apology in sequence rather than treating eventual participation as retroactive consent. A relationship dispute carries similarly clear publication limits: the person says his private affair is private, says stop, and repeatedly refuses to discuss it. The room then explores gaming, solitude, children, intimacy, conventional life and short-duration relationships. It contains a valuable internal argument that fulfillment is relative and that enjoying children does not create a duty to become a parent. It also contains peer diagnoses, pressure, absent-party allegations and deceptive dating tactics, none promoted as guidance. Sexual-health claims require correction. A speaker first says condoms are used every time, then explicitly describes condomless intercourse, bleeding and internal ejaculation. The room attributes a perceived change in attachment to mixed bodily fluids and oxytocin and advances a deterministic claim that women attach after a particular number of sexual encounters. Oxytocin participates in lactation and social processes, but the episode supplies no evidence for a sex-count threshold or inevitable attachment. Correct condom use reduces STI and pregnancy risk; it does not eliminate all risk. The long account of a guest's former relationship preserves her reported rejection, infidelity, age gap and difficulty leaving, while keeping the private former partner non-searchable and marking allegations as one-sided. The episode also records a reported sponsored trip to Israel and stereotypes about Israelis, women and Asian visitors. These remain attributable source speech, not archive facts. Opening and closing Mangchi lyrics are damaged and stay marked indistinct rather than being creatively completed. No idea has been censored or silently improved. No line-level speaker names publish until the recurring cast pass succeeds on held-out acoustic windows.

source_notes.claim: The cast's feminine presentation establishes transgender identity.
source_notes.assessment: unsupported. Gender expression is visible presentation; gender identity is an internal sense and cannot be inferred from appearance alone.

source_notes.claim: Condomless sex can be treated only as a relationship anecdote.
source_notes.assessment: unsafe. CDC says correct condom use reduces STI and pregnancy risk, though it does not eliminate all risk.

source_notes.claim: After a particular number of sexual encounters, oxytocin makes women inevitably attach.
source_notes.assessment: unsupported deterministic generalization. The episode offers no study, threshold or evidence separating hormonal effects from context, expectation and individual variation.

source_notes.claim: Going to couples therapy means the relationship is already over.
source_notes.assessment: unsupported blanket claim; preserve as opinion, not clinical guidance.

speaker_policy: Public recurring cast and guests may be identified only at episode/context level when established. Feminine performance names do not establish gender identity or stable speaker identity. Private partners, relatives and sexual-history subjects remain generic. No line-level named dialogue publishes until held-out acoustic identity windows and turn assignments pass validation.
